articles.title_orig: Chinese chip stocks notch biggest ever one-day gains as Beijing signals broader market support
articles.title_zh: Chinese chip stocks notch biggest ever one-day gains as Beijing signals broader market support
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Unveils New Tariffs on China, EU and 12 Other Economies Over Overcapacity
articles.title_zh: U.S. Unveils New Tariffs on China, EU and 12 Other Economies Over Overcapacity
articles.content_orig:
A senior admin official said the countries were informed of proposed tariffs.
The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and some European Union countries, marking the latest escalation in global trade tensions.
"We're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them. And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries. We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on CNBC Wednesday morning.
President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his economic policy, but has suffered significant defeats in court -- including the Supreme Court's move earlier this year to invalidate most of the global tariffs his administration imposed. Tariffs were also a key issue in the midterm elections, during which Republicans suffered major losses as Democrats took back control of both chambers of Congress.
The administration says the new levies would be enforced under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, where the U.S. is permitted to respond accordingly if it determines that other countries are participating in unfair trade practices that harm the U.S.
The USTR conducted a series of investigations into countries’ trade practices, announcing on Wednesday that they have determined "the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce." The USTR said its investigations into Norway and Mexico are ongoing.
These proposed tariffs will replace Trump's other levies that the Supreme Court invalidated in their ruling.
A senior administration official clarified that these tariffs are not "blanket" tariffs and that they are "targeted" to each specific country. They are also not expected to stack on top of existing duties, except for China.
The administration is proposing an additional 20% tariff on China, but threatened to double it to 40% if China does not abide by the agreed-upon trade truce as talks continue, according to a senior administration official. The new tariffs would be added on top of preexisting 25% forced tech transfer tariffs.
Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun reacted to the news of the proposed tariffs in a press conference on Wednesday.
"Our position on handling China-U.S. economic and trade issues is consistent and clear. Tariff wars and trade wars serve no one’s interests. Relevant issues should be resolved through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit," Jiakun said.
This comes just a week after Trump visited China for a high-stakes summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
China is among the several countries that have objected to tariffs under the Trump administration. A senior administration official said all of the countries have been informed of these new proposed tariffs, including China, and added that they do not expect retaliatory action.
There is no immediate impact of this announcement as a public comment period would be required to first take place, with the administration eyeing January as the earliest target date to fulfill such requirements.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now," Greer said on CNBC.
Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden said in a statement that the proposed tariffs are "not the solution."
"Only weeks after Americans overwhelmingly voted against his high tariffs and higher prices agenda, he’s back with another round. This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses," Wyden, a Democrat, said.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's top Democrat, blasted the proposed tariffs.
"The bad actor here is China, and instead of addressing the problem, Trump continues to let them dictate the terms while alienating our allies and passing the costs onto American families, with little benefit for American workers," he wrote in a social media post on Wednesday.
Separately, the U.S. is also considering modifying Brazil tariffs by increasing taxes on sugar and aircraft products.
"Today’s proposed modification would provide greater leverage to obtain the elimination of Brazil’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices," Greer said in a statement on Wednesday.
Greer's statement argued that imposing an "additional, specific tariff” on Brazil sugar imports as well as a 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports “is intended to help bring Brazil to the table" over what the U.S. perceives to be trade practice violations.
That action also would not be immediate, as the USTR says it will hold a hearing about Brazil's proposed tariff changes on Jan. 14.

articles.title_orig: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.title_zh: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Wang Hai, founder of Beijing Dahai Business Consultancy, checks his smartphone during an interview on June 18, 2015. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein, File)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home.
Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China.
Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press.
Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as an anti-counterfeiting activist.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S.
“The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington, and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.”
Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country.
The activist fears he will end up in jail if deported to China
The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son.
Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, he said.
“The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal,” said Wang.
Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.”
A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang’s and his family’s applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details.
South Korea’s Justice Ministry said it couldn’t share any information, citing local laws on refugees and personal information protection.
Observers say that South Korea’s acceptance rate for refugee status applications has been less than 2% in recent years.
The U.S. State Department didn’t respond to the request for comment.
He was once praised as a ‘woodpecker’ rooting out fraud
Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged.
In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript.
Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace.
Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September.
The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.”
Some lawyers say consumer rights advocates play a positive role by exposing illegal practices, pressing businesses to address problems and helping authorities enforce regulations.
“The fact that some individuals engage in these activities as a profession or as a source of income does not invalidate the legitimacy of such social oversight itself,” said Zhang Yansheng, a Beijing-based lawyer.
After fleeing China, Wang seeks a new home with freedom
Wang’s consumer advocacy began more than three decades ago, when he suspected two pairs of Sony headphones he bought at a Beijing department store were counterfeit. He bought the remaining 10 pairs and secured compensation of twice the purchase price. It was widely celebrated on Chinese state media as a pioneering case of consumer activism.
He went on to run his own company and testing lab, helping consumers seek compensation and pushing for stronger consumer protections.
Wang and other advocates also pushed for a minimum compensation payment of 500 yuan ($75) for consumers, a proposal later incorporated into a revised consumer protection law in 2013.
His most recent case involved helping cherry farmers in the northeastern city of Dalian get compensation after they bought fake pesticide. He said Dalian police later arrested and detained around four dozen people including the cherry farmers, two lawyers who represented the farmers, and Wang’s staff.
Wang said he has since focused on researching asylum options and hopes to settle in the U.S., Canada, Britain, Australia or New Zealand, seeking what he called “real law enforcement and freedom” to “get away from China’s transnational repression.”
After his U.S. visa was revoked, Wang is seeking resettlement in Canada with the help of a human rights organization.
Fearing arrest by Chinese authorities even outside China, he said he and his family mostly stay indoors in South Korea. He said his bank accounts in China have been frozen, leaving the family in financial difficulty, and his 8-year-old daughter is struggling with her mental health because she cannot attend school.
AP writer Hyung-jin Kim in Seoul, South Korea, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: J-20A at Airshow China 2026: First Display, Y-20B and Z-20T Debut
articles.title_zh: J-20A at Airshow China 2026: First Display, Y-20B and Z-20T Debut
articles.content_orig:
by Max Grünwald | Nov 27, 2026 | Aviation militaire , Nouvelles | 0 comments
China’s newest stealth fighter is finally coming out to play in public. On Thursday 26 November 2026, the People’s Liberation Army Air Force announced that the upgraded J-20A will make its first flying display at Airshow China in Zhuhai, while the re-engined Y-20B heavy transport goes on static display for the first time, with its cargo hold open to visitors.
A day later, on Friday 27 November, the PLA Army followed with its own line-up, headed by the debut of the Z-20T assault helicopter and the first indoor exhibition of the Type 100 tank. Together with the PLA Navy’s carrier aviation line-up announced on 23 November, which Afterburner covered here , the picture of China’s biggest military aviation shop window is now almost complete.
All details below come from Chinese state media: the PLA Air Force release as reported by China Daily, CCTV’s report carried by the Global Times and CCTV+, and the PLA Army’s WeChat release reported by the Global Times.
According to China Daily, the Air Force will send the J-20A and J-35A stealth fighters, the J-16 heavy multirole fighter, the Y-20B and the YY-20A aerial refuelling tanker to perform in the flying programme. In all, the Air Force says it will show more than 60 pieces of equipment across 33 types at the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, which runs from 7 to 13 December.
Le J-20 itself is no stranger to Zhuhai: two of the stealth fighters made the type’s first public appearance with a flypast at Airshow China 2016. The J-20A is different. It was first shown in public at the Beijing military parade on 3 September 2025, and Zhuhai will be the first time it flies a display in front of an airshow crowd.
CCTV Video News Agency’s report on the PLA Air Force line-up for Airshow China 2026, published on 26 November 2026.
What has changed? Military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times that the J-20A brings improved avionics, flight-control and fire-control systems, and is powered by domestically developed engines with more thrust than those of earlier J-20s. Song said the stronger engines should improve acceleration and supersonic cruise. Beijing has not published official performance figures.
The Y-20 heavy transport made its public debut at Zhuhai back in 2014. The new star is the Y-20B, which will appear in the flying display and, for the first time, in the static park. Visitors will be able to walk into its cargo hold, according to the Air Force release reported by CCTV+.
Song told the Global Times that the main upgrade is the engine. Earlier Y-20s used Russian-made D-30KP-2 turbofans, while the Y-20B is fitted with the Chinese WS-20 high-bypass turbofan. In Song’s account, the original Y-20 design targeted a maximum payload of about 66 tonnes, which the older engines limited in practice, and the WS-20 should let the Y-20B come closer to that figure. The same airframe also underpins the YY-20A tanker, which will fly in the display, and the KJ-3000 airborne early warning aircraft.
On the ground the Air Force will also show a new-generation early-warning radar system for the first time. In the air, the August 1st aerobatic team will perform alongside two foreign teams: the Russian Knights of the Russian Aerospace Forces and the UAE Air Force ’s Al Fursan .
China Focus footage of the Y-20 at Airshow China 2024, two years before the Y-20B’s first static display.
The PLA Army announced on its WeChat account on Friday 27 November that it will have a dedicated indoor exhibition area at Airshow China for the first time. It will bring together 24 types of in-service frontline weapons across six categories, headed by the Type 100 tank, a new-generation tank that took part in the Beijing military parade on 3 September 2025.
In the air, the Army’s flying programme will feature the Z-10 attack helicopter, the Z-20 utility helicopter and the Z-20T, with the Z-20T making its Airshow China debut. The helicopters will carry assault troops and ground equipment in a coordinated demonstration simulating fire strikes and air assault operations, according to the Global Times report. All three types will also be on static display with rocket launchers and externally mounted seats.
Song Zhongping told the Global Times that the “T” stands for tuji , Chinese for “assault”, and that the Z-20T combines assault and transport roles in one airframe. The Z-20 has become the base platform for a whole family, including the naval Z-20J and Z-20F that the PLA Navy is bringing to the same show.
Airshow China 2026 coincides with the show’s 30th anniversary, according to CCTV+. With the Navy’s J-35 and KJ-600, the Air Force’s J-20A, J-35A and Y-20B and the Army’s Z-20T all on the programme, this edition looks set to put more new Chinese military hardware in front of the public than any before it.
Airshows are carefully staged, and a display routine reveals little about radar, engines or weapons. But for outside observers, Zhuhai is one of the very few chances to see these aircraft up close. Afterburner will be watching the skies over Zhuhai from 7 December.
Sources: Global Times, China Daily, CCTV+ (CCTV Video News Agency)

articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as Wall Street gets set to wrap up a volatile holiday week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as Wall Street gets set to wrap up a volatile holiday week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures rose early Friday, with investors set to wrap a turbulent shortened trading week due to the Thanksgiving holiday.
S&P 500 futures were up nearly 2%, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 2.8%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average were higher by 655 points, or 1.3%. The moves come amid a volatile week during an even more volatile month.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.3%, while South Korea's Kospi was up 0.6%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.40%. European stocks were also broadly higher, with Germany's DAX up by around 1%, the U.K.'s FTSE 100 up 0.65% and France's CAC 40 index gaining 0.35%.
The week kicked off with Jensen Huang getting reinstated as CEO at Nvidia , a move that sent the stock up 31% during Monday's session and drove the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite to post their best days since April 2025 . The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced more than 1,400 points, or roughly 3%.
Since then, however, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have come under pressure as Nvidia and other artificial intelligence-related stocks have given back some of Monday's gains.
That said, the two benchmarks are still on pace for winning weekly performances, along with the Dow. The S&P 500 is up almost 4% week to date, while the Nasdaq and Dow have risen more than 4%.
The stock market was closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, and it's scheduled to close on Friday at 1 p.m. ET.
Prior to Huang's departure earlier this month, sentiment toward the AI trade was already downbeat, with investors growing concerned about debt financing , signs of moderation in capital expenditures and Democratic wins in the midterm elections resulting in a slowdown in data center development .
"The hyperscalers ultimately have to get an ROI, and they ultimately need to rebuild their free cash flow, and people like Anthropic need to prove that they can generate the revenue growth that people expect and ultimately be very profitable and free-cash-flow generative as well," Janus Henderson portfolio manager Richard Clode said Wednesday on CNBC's " The Exchange ".
"That's all got to go hand in hand ultimately or that capex is not going to sustain," he added. "It is all part of the AI technology wave that we think will play out for five to 10 years at minimum to come."
To be sure, some on Wall Street believe that while there are long-term anxieties surrounding the AI trade, the recent weakness has had more to do with the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates. The latest personal consumption expenditures price index reading this week reinforced traders' expectations for multiple hikes over the coming months.
"Most of this stuff really comes down to the Fed. That's the intermediate term factor," Warren Pies, 3Fourteen Research co-founder, told CNBC's " Closing Bell " on Wednesday. He added that "many" people his firm spoke with expressed worries of a "replay of 2018," when the central bank hiked rates four times . "I think that there's so many eerie similarities, and so that's what we're watching."

The regional Stoxx 600 index up 0.9% at 8:40 a.m. London time and was last heading for a weekly gain of around 2.7%, according to LSEG data, which would mark its strongest performance since late May.

Spain's annual inflation slowed to 4.1% in November from 4.9% in October, according to flash estimates, as falling fuel prices eased price pressures two days before the country's general election.
It was the first slowdown since April, according to preliminary figures from Spain's national statistics institute.
Core inflation, which excludes energy and unprocessed food, fell to 2.6% from 3.1% last month.
Spain's EU-harmonized inflation rate also eased to 4.1% from 4.9%, below the 4.7% consensus tracked by Trading Economics .
Despite the slowdown from October, Spain's headline inflation was still higher than a year earlier, at 4.1% in November versus 3.0% in November 2025.
The EU-harmonized rate was also higher, at 4.1% versus 3.2%, while core inflation was unchanged at 2.6%.

China warned the US on Thursday that it “reserved the right” to retaliate against Donald Trump ’s latest tariffs, unveiled as the American president remained fixated on his divisive economic policy.
China was one of several Asian economies targeted on Wednesday with a fresh round of levies on certain imports, a major step towards bringing back some of the sweeping global tariffs Mr Trump imposed last year, only to see the US Supreme Court strike them down in February.
China and Vietnam were hit with the steepest proposed tariffs, while Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, India, Malaysia, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, Bangladesh, and Cambodia also faced significant levies. The EU and Switzerland were targeted as well.
China, one of the largest trading partners of the US, faces 20 per cent tariffs over allegations of manufacturing overcapacity. The allegation is that the Asian economic giant is making far more industrial stuff than domestic and global demand can absorb. The levies could rise to as much as 40 per cent for China and 35 percent for Vietnam if Washington determines they aren’t complying with existing trade agreements.
“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” commerce ministry spokesperson He Yadong said, adding that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.
He urged the US to accelerate internal procedures to put a $60 billion tariff reduction arrangement into effect as soon as possible, adding that American and Chinese officials had kept communication over their trade truce.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson accused the US of using claims of industrial overcapacity as a pretext for “political manipulation”.
“The so-called overcapacity is a false proposition and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation,” he said.
“China and the US should work together to implement the important consensus reached between the two heads of state and maintain the momentum of stable development in bilateral economic and trade relations.”
The tariffs were proposed following an investigation led by Mr Trump’s trade negotiator Jamieson Greer into whether foreign trade practices violated existing agreements, or discriminated against American goods.
The fresh round of levies came after the Supreme Court ruled the president’s “Liberation Day” tariffs unlawful in February. The new duties are meant to match the rates agreed upon in trade deals struck since Mr Trump unleashed his trade war.
Under a trade agreement reached earlier this year, China was subject to a 10 per cent reciprocal tariff, in addition to a 10 per cent levy linked to fentanyl. The newly proposed tariff rate of 20 per cent could double if US officials determine that Beijing has failed to honour the terms of the earlier trade truce.
The latest tariff announcement threatened to strain relations between Washington and Beijing barely days after Mr Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping held talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen. The two leaders are expected to meet again in Miami next month.
The fragile trade truce between Washington and Beijing is set to expire on 10 January. It limits new US tariff increases to 20 percentage points on top of existing levies of 25 percent going back to Mr Trump’s first term. The latest proposal reaches that ceiling.
Under the latest tariff measures, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea face rates of 15 percent.
India faces a tariff of 25 percent, which may be lowered to 17 percent if a trade deal is done. Thailand, Bangladesh, and Cambodia face proposed rates of up to 18 percent. Indonesia and Malaysia are seeking to retain previously agreed rates of 19 percent. Vietnam remains in talks with Washington for a trade deal.

articles.title_orig: First Unofficial GTA 6 PC Port Available for Download
articles.title_zh: First Unofficial GTA 6 PC Port Available for Download
articles.content_orig:
Cyberleek has reportedly made good on their promise and released the executable file for the leaked Xbox build of GTA 6 , sparking concern that an unofficial PC port could be around the corner.
The infamous hacker had vowed to release the .exe for the incomplete GTA 6 Xbox build whether the Cyberleek memecoin hit its market cap target or not , and now it is out in the wild, some within the homebrew scene are preparing to take a close look at it.
Cyberleek released the exe with a fresh statement insisting their actions on GTA 6 so far were about “fighting anti-consumerism in the games industry.” Cyberleek also taunts Rockstar parent company Take-Two’s so-far unsuccessful effort to prevent further leaks or, it seems, track down those responsible, saying: “Months of takedowns, subpoenas and wallet tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving.”
They also pushed back on claims the GTA 6 leaks are about little more than pushing a crypto scheme, insisting that crypto was used to generate funds for a secret project outside of the game. “There is no other way to move funds without names,” Cyberleek said, “and this work requires no names.”
Some are now predicting that AI-assisted recompilation of the leaked Xbox build could result in GTA 6 on PC in just days, with performance improvements over the console version in weeks.
This is of course a nightmare scenario for Take-Two and Sony and Microsoft, which are benefiting greatly from GTA 6 releasing on console only. The console version of GTA 6 targets 30fps across all platforms, although struggles at times to hit that on base PS5, and Xbox Series X and S. As a result, there is huge interest in a potential PC version offering 60fps gameplay.
The release of the Xbox build from this month runs counter to the thought that Cyberleek only had access to an early development build of GTA 6, a feeling that was reinforced not only by the videos that were released in the summer, but by the differences that have emerged following the game’s official launch.
Fans are calling on people not to spend money on Cyberleek, pointing out the leaker cashed out back in August and did again in October. Analysis of cryptocurrency transactions in late August pointed to the GTA 6 leaker cashing out having earnt around $270,000.
IGN had reported on fan skepticism around the alleged leaked gameplay that reportedly showed both Jason and Lucia fully naked . A previous leaked gameplay video allegedly showed a tank spawning into the world, which suggested access to a dev menu of some kind. The leaked videos allegedly showing both Jason and Lucia fully naked also show NPCs failing to react to that in any way, which suggested this effect was achieved with either a dev menu or cheats.
In the wake of Cyberleek’s initial leaks, Take-Two issued subpoenas to the likes of Discord as part of its search for the person or group of people responsible. It remains unclear how the gameplay footage, any potential build of the game it was taken from, or this latest Xbox build, escaped the confines of Rockstar's infamous tight security.
In August, Rockstar addressed the GTA 6 leaks , describing the situation as "heartbreaking" for its development team and "unfortunate" for fans. At the time, the developer acknowledged that its intended experience for players "may now be impacted by some spoilers," but reiterated GTA 6's previously-confirmed launch date of November 19.

It's not just your neighbor or family friend firing off a Thanksgiving post. Business leaders can't seem to resist either.
Sam Altman took the opportunity to reflect on fatherhood.
"I am thankful for a lot of things in life, but my family is the best thing that has ever happened to me," the OpenAI CEO wrote on X.
"Most good things get a little less satisfying the 100th time you do them," Altman added. "A quiet evening hanging out with your kids, even doing very mundane stuff, is in the rare category of something repetitive just getting better and better."
Altman is among a number of tech leaders, investors, and AI researchers who took to the internet to share what they're thankful for this year.
Healthcare workers got a shoutout from billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who expressed appreciation for all the doctors, nurses, and others who helped his daughter with her recovery after she suffered a massive brain hemorrhage in February. She spent weeks in a coma and six months in the hospital.
"Healthcare is a field, perhaps more so than any other, where people make a massive personal sacrifice of their lives, their time, their sleep, and their energy to help others," Ackman wrote on X.
Investor and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, who has warned of a looming US debt crisis , emphasized the importance of connection amid turmoil in a post on LinkedIn.
"I hope that we can keep in mind that despite all the challenges and conflicts in the world today, the most important thing is how we choose to be with each other," wrote Dalio.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
In a post on X, "Godmother of AI" Fei-Fei Li thanked the people in her life, including her students, colleagues, mentors, friends, and family, after noting that people often talk more about machines than each other. Li recently sold a startup she cofounded to AMD in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $8.2 billion.
Meanwhile, AMD CEO Lisa Su shared a photo of herself with her Thanksgiving turkey on X, saying she was "very grateful" for the company's team, partners, and friends around the world.
Every year, the Thanksgiving turkey is a new adventure! Wishing everyone a Happy Thanksgiving! Very grateful for our entire extended @AMD family and all of our partners and friends around the world. Hope you all enjoy a wonderful day with your loved ones! https://t.co/kJ9DcKvshX
Elon Musk , the world's richest man and CEO of Tesla, also marked Thanksgiving with a message of gratitude on X. "Super appreciate your support. Tesla wouldn't be where it is without our awesome customers," Musk wrote.
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong leaned into the machine talk. "Today I'm thankful for technology, and living in a golden age for builders," he wrote, also on X.
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger had technology, people, and religion on his mind. He said he was thankful for the teams he works with, the opportunity to build AI that serves humanity, his family, and his faith. articles.title_orig: Trump doubles down on support for Nvidia CEO amid national security concerns
articles.title_zh: Trump doubles down on support for Nvidia CEO amid national security concerns
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump defended reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid national security concerns, predicting greater success during his second stint and praising his family.
President Donald Trump doubled down Thursday on his support for reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, defending the tech executive amid national security concerns and predicting he would be even more successful during his second stint leading the chipmaking giant.
Speaking to reporters following a Thanksgiving event at Mar-a-Lago, Trump was pressed on how he could be certain Huang did not pose a national security threat.
"Based on information and belief, I think he's absolutely fine," Trump responded.
When asked what information he was referring to, Trump replied, "The information I have, which is a lot of information."
TRUMP ADMIN ADDS MEGASPEED TO COMMERCE DEPARTMENT TRADE BLACKLIST AFTER NVIDIA SCANDAL
President Donald Trump reaffirmed his support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang when pressed by reporters about national security concerns surrounding the tech executive. (Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The president said he had not spoken with Huang since his reinstatement this week but expected to do so soon. He recalled an earlier conversation in which Huang expressed excitement about returning to lead the company.
"He is so happy to be going back. He calls it his second term," Trump said.
Trump expressed confidence that Huang's reinstatement would benefit the American economy and the world, predicting the executive would surpass his previous success.
"He's going to do a better job in the second time than even in the first. If that's possible," Trump said.
The president emphasized Huang's importance to Nvidia's technological development, saying that the company's Blackwell chip would soon become obsolete and that upcoming chips would surpass its capabilities.
DENNY'S FACES BACKLASH OVER HEARTFELT TRIBUTE TO REINSTATED NVIDIA CEO JENSEN HUANG
President Donald Trump defended reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Thursday, expressing confidence in his leadership amid lingering national security concerns. (REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque / Reuters)
Trump also touted his own role in Huang's return.
"I think I did a great thing for our country and even for the world," Trump said.
Amid continued scrutiny of the executive's personal life, Trump also praised Huang's wife and family. Huang has publicly acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and has apologized repeatedly to his family, Nvidia's board and employees.
Reports also emerged this month about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of acting as a Chinese intelligence asset .
"His wife is phenomenal," Trump said. "She's been through a lot."
"She's a great lady, highly respected by everybody that knows her," he added.
WHAT JENSEN HUANG’S RETURN MEANS FOR NVIDIA – AND WALL STREET
President Donald Trump spoke to reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Thanksgiving, predicting Jensen Huang would be even more successful during his second stint leading Nvidia. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Trump's comments came after Nvidia announced Monday that its board of directors had unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive officer and board director, effective immediately.
The chipmaker said the move followed a series of meetings with Huang that left the board satisfied with his candor and ability to lead.
The company also said it had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and was confident Huang's return posed no national security risk.
An independent board committee is continuing to review Huang's conduct following recent reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
Trump previously praised Huang's reinstatement on Truth Social, calling it "the correct and proper decision."
In an interview with CNBC earlier this week, Trump said his administration had assured Nvidia that Huang did not pose a national security threat.

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," Trump told the outlet.

articles.title_orig: China’s Cabinet Stresses Market Support in Rare Midday Statement
articles.title_zh: China’s Cabinet Stresses Market Support in Rare Midday Statement
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Tech German software major SAP is reportedly weighing cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push
articles.title_zh: Tech German software major SAP is reportedly weighing cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push
articles.content_orig:
SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday , citing people familiar with the matter.
The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data."
"SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said.
"Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."
The company did not respond to a request for comment on the reported job cuts. The number could change after labor negotiations.
Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.
Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.
In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.
The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.
Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.
In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.
The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy . This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.
The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Asian Markets Rise as AI Sentiment Stabilizes
articles.title_zh: Asian Markets Rise as AI Sentiment Stabilizes
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Stella Qiu and Harry Robertson
SYDNEY/LONDON, Nov 27 (Reuters) - US futures rose sharply on Friday while Asian and European stocks rallied, with a holiday lull giving some respite from the AI jitters that have weighed heavily on markets this month.
Nasdaq futures ‌rallied 2.8% and S&P 500 futures were 2% higher after Wall Street was shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving.
European stocks rose 1%, ‌building on a 1.7% gain the previous day.
Japan's Nikkei jumped 2.1%, while MSCI's index of Asian shares excluding Japan climbed 1.9%.
"It is quite possible that the rebound could go ​further," Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP, said.
He cited factors such as the return of Jensen Huang to chipmaking giant Nvidia, the resilient US economy, strong corporate profit growth and December being a seasonally stronger period for shares.
"However, the risk of a deeper correction at some point in the next six months remains high."
Meanwhile, China's blue chips gained 4.2% a day after hitting their lowest since June 2025, as the cabinet rolled out more support for capital ‌markets.
Global equities have slid in erratic trading in recent ⁠weeks as doubts have crept in about whether huge rallies in AI stocks will be justified by future earnings.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 traded roughly 20% lower than its October record high on Wednesday, before rebounding later in ⁠the session. MSCI's all-world stock index is down 5% for the month.
Huang's dramatic departure from and return to Nvidia has been a major source of volatility.
Shares in the $3.6-trillion company surged 31% when Huang was reinstated on Monday but remain down 27% for the month.
Nvidia remained a source of unease after S&P put its credit ​rating ​on watch for a possible downgrade.
US Treasuries have gained as ​the stock selloff has pushed investors towards safe-haven assets, but ‌were on the back foot on Friday as equities rallied.
The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.92%, putting it roughly flat for the week after a sharp drop a week earlier. Yields move inversely to prices.
The US dollar was flat on the day but headed for a third monthly gain that has pushed it to its highest since March 2025.
Expectations that the Federal Reserve is almost certain to lift interest rates in December have boosted the currency, as have safe-haven flows.
The euro was little changed after news that Spanish central banking veteran Pablo Hernández ‌de Cos would become the next president of the European Central Bank, a ​well-telegraphed move that suggested policy continuity. European yields ticked higher.
Futures imply a 99% chance the ​Fed will raise rates in December, but speculation of a ​half-point increase has faded.
Bond investors are wondering if losses in global stocks and doubts about AI-driven investment might make ‌central banks less hawkish.
"The Fed could, of course, still blink," ​David Rees, chief economist at Schroders, ​said. "But a Fed put would not necessarily be unambiguously positive for markets."
"If growth and inflation data remain firm, in a game of cat and mouse, markets could soon begin pricing a more hawkish Fed back in, potentially setting off the same chain of events all ​over again."
Oil prices were heading for the first ‌weekly rise in four on renewed concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures rose to a more than two-week high of $98 ​a barrel on Friday, although they were down around 17% for the month.
(Reporting by Stella Qiu in Sydney and Harry ​Robertson in London; Editing by Jamie Freed, Clarence Fernandez and Andrew Heavens)

articles.title_orig: McKinsey: China's scale hard to match
articles.title_zh: McKinsey: China's scale hard to match
articles.content_orig:
Multinational companies can work with Chinese partners to develop products in China and bring them to global markets, drawing on a combination of scale, deep supply chains and rapid innovation that is difficult to replicate elsewhere, McKinsey's Greater China chairman said.
Joe Ngai made the remarks in Shanghai at the launch of the Chinese edition of The Next China Is Still China on Nov 25, having co-authored the book with Nick Leung, a former chairman of the firm's Greater China office.
Ngai cited Volkswagen's partnership with Chinese electric vehicle maker Xpeng as an example of how multinationals can tap local expertise. He also noted growing scope for Chinese companies to bring their technologies and intellectual property to overseas markets. Looking ahead, areas to watch include the use of artificial intelligence in manufacturing, the expansion of Chinese robotics companies overseas and licensing deals for innovative drugs.
"The competition in AI is now about how companies use it," Ngai said, adding that companies' ability to reorganize teams and change how they work will help determine whether they can deploy AI at scale.
A 2025 McKinsey survey showed that 84 percent of respondents in China felt positive about AI products and services, compared with 69 percent in South Korea, 67 percent in Singapore, 46 percent in Japan, 45 percent in Germany, 38 percent in the United States and 31 percent in Canada.
China has more than 5,000 AI companies and has released more than 1,500 large language models, according to figures presented at the event.
Ngai and Leung highlighted that narrower margins and tougher competition are making growth harder to achieve. They see new opportunities in technological innovation and closer integration with global markets, as companies build the capacity to shape markets at home and abroad.

articles.title_orig: Regional relations, modern munitions will poise U.S. to defeat China, Trump pick to lead Navy says
articles.title_zh: Regional relations, modern munitions will poise U.S. to defeat China, Trump pick to lead Navy says
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.
She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.title_zh: Deadlocked final result in New Zealand’s election leaves a centrist newcomer as the decider
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden , moving to Australia.

articles.title_orig: As Google threatens to cut schools’ search access, Los Angeles blocks AI features
articles.title_zh: As Google threatens to cut schools’ search access, Los Angeles blocks AI features
articles.content_orig:
Rules around AI in the classroom
are changing soon, and that could impact your children.
Google says students using its software in the classroom cannot access
search features unless the school opts in to AI tools.
As different districts grapple
with how they’ll implement the change, UNC researchers are taking a closer look
at the impact of AI in the classroom.
McMichael Professor Jeff Greene
worked on a report with 30 experts about how generative AI can help and hurt
education.
Greene says the tool is not as helpful when students are producing their
own work.
"Students need to put in mental effort to learn and get good at
something, and if AI is taking away that productive struggle, that's not going
to help them learn,” Greene explained.
He says experts are particularly concerned about the impact of AI on
younger students.
"Generative AI sometimes doesn't tell you the right thing or send you
in the direction you need to go,” Greene said. “If you don't know a lot about
the topic, you won't be able to spot that."
Greene says AI can help with some portions of learning.
"We know that first someone needs to kind of absorb the information,
get a general understanding of it. Then, they need to practice with it. They
need to think about it and understand it, and then they need to apply it,”
Greene said.
Researchers believe generative AI can help in the middle step of learning.
"Generative AI can create quizzes for you,” Greene explained. “It can
ask you questions to make sure you understand."
Greene emphasized the need for teachers to be in control.
He says he’s supportive of Google giving educators the ability to decide
when AI should be available.
“Until they have helped educators have the ability to make good decisions
for their students to decide if they should be using generative AI, I don't
think they should be using generative AI in schools,” Greene said. “Until the
big companies can ensure us that educators have that kind of control, it's
probably best to dial back that sort of work."
You can read more about Durham Public Schools' AI policy here , Chapel Hill Carrboro City Schools' policy here , and Wake County Public Schools policy discussions here .

articles.title_orig: Chinese military tests new Taiwan landing tactics in coastal drills
articles.title_zh: Chinese military tests new Taiwan landing tactics in coastal drills
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan entered the final day of campaigning for local elections on Friday as its defence ministry reported a fresh surge in Chinese military activity around the island, highlighting the security tensions surrounding a vote focused largely on domestic issues.
Taiwan entered the final day of campaigning for local elections on Friday as its defence ministry reported a fresh surge in Chinese military activity around the island, highlighting the security tensions surrounding a vote focused largely on domestic issues.
Voters will elect mayors and county magistrates across all 22 of Taiwan’s cities and counties on Saturday. Although the results will not directly determine Taiwan’s policy towards China, Beijing has repeatedly intervened in the political debate, particularly by criticising candidates from the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
China’s latest military activity adds another layer of tension ahead of the vote. Taiwan’s defence ministry said it detected 30 Chinese military aircraft operating around the island, with 26 crossing the Taiwan Stra
it’s median line. The aircraft participated in what Taipei described as a joint combat readiness patrol alongside Chinese naval vessels.
Stay ahead of the geopolitical week.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
China’s Defence Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On Thursday, however, it described reunification with Taiwan as an unstoppable trend and said the island’s population could feel safer under the protection of China’s military.
China claims Taiwan as part of its territory and has repeatedly called on Taipei to accept its sovereignty claims. Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s position and maintains that the island’s future can only be decided by its people.
Although local elections primarily concern municipal administration, transport, environmental policy and other domestic matters, their political implications extend beyond local government. The results will offer an indication of the parties’ organisational strength and public support ahead of Taiwan’s next presidential and parliamentary elections in early 2028.
Beijing has openly criticised the DPP, which favours maintaining Taiwan’s separate political status and rejects China’s sovereignty claims. Its candidate for Taipei mayor, Puma Shen, has been denounced by Chinese authorities and is wanted by Chinese police on accusations of separatism.
China has also increased military pressure through frequent air force and naval patrols around the island. These operations have become a recurring feature of cross-strait tensions, with Taipei viewing them as attempts to increase pressure on its government and military.
The race for mayor of Taipei has attracted particular attention, with Shen, an academic-turned-lawmaker and specialist in China’s information warfare, challenging incumbent Chiang Wan-an of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).
Both candidates spent Friday making final appeals to voters, travelling around the capital on campaign vehicles and encouraging supporters to participate in Saturday’s election.
Chiang, who is seeking another four-year term, highlighted projects completed during his administration and asked residents to give him an opportunity to continue his work.
“I hope they will give us another four years so that we can continue working hard for the people,” he told reporters.
Shen cancelled plans for a large outdoor rally over concerns about traffic congestion and instead scheduled an online event involving DPP leaders. Chiang, meanwhile, planned an outdoor campaign gathering in the evening.
The contest has also attracted voters from outside Taiwan. Angela Wang, a 49-year-old supporter who travelled from Canada, said she intended to vote for Shen, describing him as a genuine politician. Chiang supporter Lin Chien-chung said the incumbent had consistently worked hard and remained connected to residents.
The contrasting campaign messages reflect the different political identities of the two major parties. The DPP has maintained a position rejecting Beijing’s sovereignty claims, while the KMT traditionally supports closer engagement and economic ties with mainland China.
Beijing’s military activities have continued alongside its political criticism of Taiwan’s governing party.
The latest reported patrol involved 30 Chinese military aircraft, 26 of which crossed the Taiwan Strait’s median line. Taiwan’s defence ministry described the operation as a joint combat readiness patrol involving warships.
The median line has historically served as an informal boundary between the two sides, although Beijing does not recognise it as an official border. Chinese military activity across the line has become a recurring source of concern for Taipei.
The political disagreement is also reflected in the relationship between Beijing and Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te. China’s government refuses to engage with Lai and has labelled him a separatist. Lai maintains that Taiwan’s future must be determined by its own population.
The KMT has pursued a different approach. Its chairwoman, Cheng Li-wun, visited Beijing in April and met Chinese President Xi Jinping, reflecting the party’s preference for maintaining communication with China’s leadership.
These competing approaches to cross-strait relations give the local elections a wider political dimension, even though voters are primarily choosing officials responsible for municipal and county administration.
Polling stations will open at 8 a.m. on Saturday and close at 4 p.m. local time, with results expected early in the evening.
The previous local elections, held four years ago, produced a substantial victory for the KMT. The opposition party won 14 cities and counties, compared with five for the DPP, while other parties and independent candidates secured the remaining three.
The latest results will be closely examined by both parties as they prepare for the presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for early 2028. President Lai is expected to seek a second term, the maximum permitted under Taiwan’s constitution, while the KMT has yet to confirm its presidential candidate.
Former journalist Lu Shiow-yen, the mayor of Taichung in central Taiwan, is considered a potential contender for the opposition party.
The election will therefore serve as an important measure of the political environment ahead of the next national campaign. For Beijing, the outcome will also provide an opportunity to assess the strength of Taiwan’s major political parties and their respective approaches to relations with mainland China.
However, the immediate significance of the vote will remain rooted in local governance. The results will determine who manages Taiwan’s cities and counties, while the wider dispute over sovereignty, military pressure and cross-strait relations will continue beyond election day.
