Russiaâs Vladimir Putin has been abandoned by one of the worldâs premier dictators amid a diplomatic loversâ tiff.
North Koreaâs Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un has furnished Moscow with its troops and munitions in the fight against Ukraine , with his soldiers clandestinely shipped west to the edge of Europe, where they fought inside Russiaâs borders to repel Kyivâs incursions and counterattacks.
Russia and North Korea's relationship has posed an uneasy proposition for the West.
But that backscratching has now ended, Ukrainian intelligence claims, after Pyongyang said it will cease military aid to Moscow.
It is also terminating deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery ammunition.
Kim walks by a memorial to North Korean troops killed in Russia.
Ukraineâs Main Directorate of Intelligence said Thursday that North Koreaâs feathers were ruffled by Moscow when it proposed de-escalation in tensions between North Korea and South Korea.
Ukraine said that the halt order was personally issued by Kim.
Could the bromance be in danger?
According to the Kyiv Post , the order came after Andrey Rudenko, the Russian Deputy Foreign Minister, said that his country planned to seek de-escalation on the Korean peninsula.
North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son-ui said Moscowâs request raised questions about alliances and relations with South Korea.
The two countries have a mutual agreement in place.
Alexander Kazakov/via REUTERS
The withdrawal of ammunition poses a substantial problem for Moscow. Ukrainian intelligence said that ammo from the isolationist dictatorship accounted for between 25 percent and 40 percent of those used by Russia, according to a Kyiv Post report from July.
According to the Post, there is no suggestion that the existing troops drafted in to help Russia are being pulled away. Rather, Moscowâs request for additional troops, bumping numbers from 8,500 to 50,000, is being stalled.
North Korea has sent thousands of troops to assist Russia.
In 2025, Pyongyang acknowledged its troops had been deployed to help repel Ukraineâs Kursk offensive.
North Korea has also banned Russian military aircraft from its airspace, in addition to munitions withdrawals.
The two leaders have long aligned on the world stage.
Sergey Bobylev/via REUTERS
South Korea is aligned with much of Europe and the West in its support for Ukraine and in its condemnation of Russia following its full-scale invasion in 2022.
However, South Koreaâs imports of Russian coal rose 35 percent in 2026 compared to last year, according to The Post.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX shares jump 4% amid tech rally and after Musk says he will expand on Trump Account share donations
articles.title_zh: SpaceX shares jump 4% amid tech rally and after Musk says he will expand on Trump Account share donations
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares rose in premarket trading amid a broader tech rally and after CEO Elon Musk expanded his SpaceX share-donation plan for U.S. children.
Big Tech stocks, including Nvidia , Intel, Marvell , AMD and Micron were all higher in premarket trading as the sector rebounded from a heavy selloff earlier this week.
SpaceX had jumped more than 7% in overnight trading on Blue Ocean ATS after Musk posted about donating shares on X.
"I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year," Musk said in the post .
Blue Ocean ATS is an alternative trading system for U.S. equities that operates from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, outside regular U.S. stock market hours. According to the platform's holiday schedule , overnight trading resumed at 8 p.m. ET on Thanksgiving Day. U.S. stock exchanges were closed Thursday and are scheduled to close early Friday.
SpaceX stock was last 4% higher in premarket trading. Shares closed 1.30% higher on Wednesday ahead of Thanksgiving.
The latest pledge follows SpaceX's announcement Wednesday that it would donate one share of its Class A stock to every active Trump Account, tax-advantaged investment account for American children, with Musk personally matching the gift.
In a separate post on X, Musk said SpaceX's contribution would be transferred next month, while his personal donation would follow when his lockup period expires in June next year.
Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created as of October, according to the White House.
Since the program's launch in July, families and friends have contributed more than $1 billion to the accounts, bringing total deposits from all sources to more than $9 billion, CNBC reported earlier this week.

Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home.
Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China.
Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press.
Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as anti-counterfeiting activist.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S.
“The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington , and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.”
Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country.
The activist fears he will end up in jail if deported to China
The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son.
Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, according to him.
“The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal," said Wang.
Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.”
A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang's and his family's applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details.
The U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to the request for comment.
He was once praised as a ‘woodpecker’ rooting out fraud
Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged.
In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript.
Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace.
Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September.
The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.”
Some lawyers say consumer rights advocates play a positive role by exposing illegal practices, pressing businesses to address problems and helping authorities enforce regulations.
“The fact that some individuals engage in these activities as a profession or as a source of income does not invalidate the legitimacy of such social oversight itself,” said Zhang Yansheng, a Beijing-based lawyer.
After fleeing China, Wang seeks a new home with freedom
Wang’s consumer advocacy began more than three decades ago, when he suspected two pairs of Sony headphones he bought at a Beijing department store were counterfeit. He bought the remaining 10 pairs and secured compensation of twice the purchase price. It was widely celebrated on Chinese state media as a pioneering case of consumer activism.
He went on to run his own company and testing lab, helping consumers seek compensation and pushing for stronger consumer protections.
Wang and other advocates also pushed for a minimum compensation payment of 500 yuan ($75) for consumers, a proposal later incorporated into a revised consumer protection law in 2013.
His most recent case involved helping cherry farmers in the northeastern city of Dalian get compensation after they bought fake pesticide. He said Dalian police later arrested and detained around four dozens of people including the cherry farmers, two lawyers who represented the farmers, and Wang's staff.
Wang said he has since focused on researching asylum options and hopes to settle in the U.S., Canada, Britain, Australia or New Zealand, seeking what he called “real law enforcement and freedom” to “get away from China's transnational repression.”
After his U.S. visa was revoked, Wang is seeking resettlement in Canada with the help of a human rights organization.
Fearing arrest by Chinese authorities even outside China, he said he and his family mostly stay indoors in South Korea. He said his bank accounts in China have been frozen, leaving the family in financial difficulty, and his 8-year-old daughter is struggling with her mental health because she cannot attend school.

articles.title_orig: Two Italians killed in Kuwait drone attack; Trump says Iran war ends ‘whenever I want it’
articles.title_zh: Two Italians killed in Kuwait drone attack; Trump says Iran war ends ‘whenever I want it’
articles.content_orig:
Two Italians have been killed after an alleged Iranian attack on Kuwait, Kuwaiti forces said Thursday.
In a post on X , Kuwait's army said the deaths followed Iranian attacks on the country, with the two Italians killed by falling missile debris. Two others were also injured.
In response, a spokesperson for Iran's military told state media that no offensive or military operations had been carried out in the area and that "these accusations should be viewed as a cover for continued malevolence and an attempt to exacerbate insecurity in the region" by U.S. and Israeli forces.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Telegram that he had spoken with his Italian counterpart, Antonio Tajani, and expressed regret over their deaths, while stressing that Tehran had no role or involvement in the incident.
"The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war," Araghchi wrote on X.
He also said Iran was ready to cooperate with the governments of Kuwait and Italy in investigating the incident.
Separately, Israel said Thursday that it was prepared to carry out strikes against Iran "at any moment," even without U.S. forces joining the effort, according to Israeli military spokesman Effie Defrin on Israeli broadcaster Kan .
The comments came after U.S. envoy Jared Kushner told a podcast Wednesday that Israel "needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset."
Israel has been pushing the Trump administration to back another offensive against Tehran, with Reuters reporting on Nov. 18 that Israeli spy chief Roman Gofman pushed for joint strikes when he met U.S. officials earlier in the month.
Late Thursday, President Donald Trump said on PBS that the U.S. had "victory at hand" in the Iran conflict and reiterated that victory would come "whenever I want it to be, to be honest."
Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with U.S. military personnel, Trump said Washington was still trying to give Iran "every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives."
But he added that he was not sure whether Tehran would agree.
"Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are," Trump said.

articles.title_orig: Putin's grip on Crimea tested amid major blackout as Zelenskyy warns of looming Russian strike

A large-scale power outage hit Russian-occupied Crimea on Nov. 26, temporarily leaving Sevastopol without electricity and disrupting public transport in several cities, Russian-installed authorities and local media reported.
The outage comes amid weeks of electricity shortages across the illegally Russian-annexed Crimean Peninsula , with Russian-installed authorities blaming damage to power lines outside Crimea for disruptions that have forced rolling blackouts and affected public transport.
Russian-installed energy provider Sevastopolenergo said the outage was caused by an incident at power facilities outside the region, adding that specialists were gradually restoring electricity to socially significant facilities based on available grid capacity.
Electricity restrictions had already been introduced across the peninsula on Nov. 25, with Russian-installed authorities citing emergency maintenance and repair work, warning that the measures could last up to 10 days.
The latest outage adds to the growing logistical difficulties facing Russian-occupied Crimea, as the peninsula becomes increasingly isolated.
On Nov. 17, Ukrainian forces destroyed a section of the Crimean Bridge's road span, cutting road traffic across the crossing. Two days later, another strike damaged its railway tracks, temporarily halting train traffic.
Fuel shortages have also affected the peninsula, with fuel purchase limits imposed at gas stations in occupied Sevastopol after the Crimean Bridge strikes triggered queues and fears of supply disruptions.
Léopold Rannou is a breaking news reporter on the war desk at the Kyiv Independent. Before joining the newsroom, he worked as a reporter for Editorial Perfil, an Argentine newspaper based in Buenos Aires, where he covered geopolitics and international affairs. He holds a master in management from HEC Paris and a bachelor’s degree in philosophy from Sorbonne University.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "trying to support" NABU and SAPO, "but not to the extent of breaking the law, as they are independent institutions."
Russian forces launched 155 drones, including 83 jet-powered ones, Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoys at Ukraine overnight on Nov. 27, the Air Force said.
The number includes 2,262 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyayev said on Telegram that Russian air defenses had downed four Ukrainian drones over the region, adding that the threat of further drone attacks remained.
A NATO official speaking on condition of anonymity told Politico that both sides had agreed to the original statement, indicating that Trump had subsequently changed the wording unilaterally.
Zelensky also expressed frustration over delays in American deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors, saying Ukraine continued to face a severe shortage of missiles capable of stopping Russian ballistic attacks.
Russian border guards, operating under Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), have helped protect Armenia's borders with Turkey and Iran under a bilateral agreement signed in 1992.
The man received emergency medical assistance and was taken to the hospital with severe burns. He remains in intensive care, according to the Ukrainian embassy.
"Following my meeting with the Prime Minister of Hungary and, more broadly, what has effectively been a reset in relations between Hungary and Ukraine, our neighbors have joined our global coalition," President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Under Briukhovetsky's leadership, the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy broke with the Soviet model of education in Ukraine, and became one of the country's most respected educational institutions.
A Ukrainian civil society source familiar with the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that representatives of the European Commission have succumbed to the Ukrainian authorities' pressure and agreed that "it was inappropriate to give international experts a decisive role in the selection of Supreme Court judges."

articles.title_orig: Trump demands investigation into GDP data revisions
articles.title_zh: Trump demands investigation into GDP data revisions
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."
Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate . That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.
That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post , suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections , where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.
"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.
However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.
On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.
The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.
Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary . Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.
GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.
The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.
Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.
Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."
"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.
Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool . They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Global stocks rally on AI rebound after bruising month, while Treasuries dip
articles.title_zh: Global stocks rally on AI rebound after bruising month, while Treasuries dip
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off.
"The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification."
But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent."
"Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said.
The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India.
Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative."
"European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending."
U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities.
But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

articles.title_orig: Denny's faces backlash over heartfelt tribute to reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Denny's faces backlash over heartfelt tribute to reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him.
The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13.
"Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X .
The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993.
The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed.
"We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.
Huang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies.
The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history.
Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker.
While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee.
"Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

articles.content_orig:
• Beast in the East: A massive Thanksgiving storm that spans from Missouri to Massachusetts has knocked out power for more than 900,000 customers , flooded coastal communities and shut down some East Coast bridges and roadways . Water rose to record highs on the Mid-Atlantic coast , and snow blanketed parts of the Midwest before shifting south.
• Air travel snags: Hundreds more flights have been canceled or delayed today after weather disrupted the busy pre-Thanksgiving travel period . Here’s what to do if your flight is delayed.
• Parade paused: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed for the first time in its history. Americans who enjoy the tradition on TV will have to wait until Saturday, while New Yorkers made the most of the unusually empty streets this morning.
Heavy rain and strong winds hit the East Coast Thursday, putting a snag in some Americans’ Thanksgiving Day plans .
Trees came down onto houses and cars in Washington D.C., Maryland and elsewhere, prompting first responders to rescue motorists and evacuate residents.
Drivers tried to make their way through streets filled with floodwaters in New Jersey, and gusty winds battered pedestrians in New York City, where the iconic Macy’s parade was postponed due to the weather.
Thanksgiving may have just gotten more stressful for hundreds of thousands of Americans as a storm sweeps across the Midwest and East Coast, causing power outages .
Thanksgiving may have just gotten a bit more stressful for more than 850,000 Americans as a storm sweeps across the Midwest and East Coast causing power outages.
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a ground stop for Delta Air Lines flights headed to New York’s LaGuardia Airport until 7:30 p.m. ET.
Carrier-requested ground stops are often used by airlines to pause incoming aircraft so they can avoid traffic jams and get caught up with the planes already on the ground.
An earlier ground stop for all flights heading to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport was canceled after about an hour when the FAA reported its objectives had been met.
Meanwhile, an elevated monorail connecting the terminals at Newark Liberty International Airport was shut down due to concerns over high winds . Buses will replace the Air Train, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said.
And in Miami, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 cargo plane that skidded off the runway has been removed, the FAA reported in an operations update. That runway has been out of service since the incident, causing some delays.It should reopen within 48 hours, the agency said.
Floodwaters in Atlantic City, New Jersey, are starting to recede after the storm brought major flooding Thursday, the city’s emergency management coordinator said.
“Things are winding down in the city, although we are still experiencing some water in the streets,” Scott Evans said in a video posted to the city government’s Facebook page . “But the city is in the de-watering process, and the city is draining.”
Some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, Evans said. Emergency crews helped residents evacuate several homes and carried out more than 14 rescues involving vehicles stuck in deep water, he said.
“We were in major flooding today, so there is some damage out there,” Evans said, adding that officials will assess the damage soon. “We didn’t see the highest levels that we thought we might see, but the the potential was there.”
Some roads are still closed but are expected to reopen in the coming hours.
The East Coast storm continues to take shape this evening, centered just off the Mid-Atlantic coast. Snow has blanketed parts of the Midwest and Ohio Valley while heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding pushed into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.
East Coast: Heavy rain and gusty winds are in full force across the Northeast but are beginning to taper across the Mid-Atlantic, though a few showers could linger into the evening. Conditions are deteriorating in New England and will reach their worst overnight.
Another round of coastal flooding will arrive as high tide approaches but, for most areas, won’t be as extreme.
🌧️ Get your local forecast and more in the CNN Weather app ☔️
Midwest: Snow has almost entirely tapered off in Missouri and Illinois after significant snow fell overnight Wednesday, though rain still lingers. Parts of southeast Missouri, western Kentucky and western Tennessee will continue to see a mixed bag of rain and snow through this afternoon. A few inches of snow has already fallen in parts of eastern Tennessee. Wet conditions will begin to taper off this evening.
Great Lakes and Ohio Valley: Rain and wintry precipitation is ongoing from central Tennessee to central Michigan. In parts of central and northern Tennessee, rain has transitioned to wet snow and a few inches will accumulate as temperatures drop . Rain and snow will persist into Friday evening, tapering off overnight.
An ice arena was damaged during a winter storm in the city of Wentzville, Missouri, about 40 miles west of St. Louis, the city said .
The area received major snowfall Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day.
The arena is closed until further notice while the damage is assessed, the mayor said.
As heavy rain and fierce wind continues to lash the Mid-Atlantic Coast, officials in several Virginia cities say emergency response teams have rescued people from high waters.
Norfolk Fire-Rescue crews performed 39 rescues as of 3:15 p.m. Thursday, a city spokesperson told CNN in a statement. Nearby Virginia Beach has also seen damage from the storm .
There were no injuries related to the water rescues, the spokesperson added. Two dogs were also rescued. The city previously said one person rescued was taken to the hospital, but later said the hospitalization was due to an unrelated incident.
Rising waters have also led to rescues in Poquoson, Virginia, a coastal city about 35 miles north of Norfolk. Around five people had been rescued from their homes as of about 3:15 p.m., according to the city’s fire chief, Mike Bryant.
No injuries were reported, Bryant said, and individuals were all taken to homes of family members less affected by the flooding.
This post has been updated with more information.

Though family and friends across the country are still feasting on Thanksgiving dinner (or in a post-meal food coma), a storm that could disrupt weekend travel plans across the country is already taking shape.
A weather system that’s set to bring even more rain and snow to the Pacific Northwest Friday night will dive south into the central US, spreading snow across the central Rockies.
The storm will then bring wet weather to the central Plains and Midwest Saturday afternoon and evening.
But the real trouble is likely to set in Sunday morning — typically the busiest travel day of the year — as the storm intensifies and brings the potential of heavy rain and gusty winds from the Louisiana Gulf Coast to southern Michigan.
The system will quickly scoot east and could complicate travel across the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Sunday afternoon. Evening travel is going to cut it close in the Northeast as the storm swiftly approaches late in the day Sunday.
A second, stronger storm will also approach the West Coast Saturday night, likely impacting travel from eastern Washington to the Bay Area. Rain could spread as far south as Southern California.

Add Axios as your preferred source to

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and President Trump speak to reporters aboard Air Force One. Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.
Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.
Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of  a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.
Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.
The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.
What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.
Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

articles.title_orig: China threatened the US with a response to the new tariffs – what is at stake for the trade truce between Beijing and Washington
articles.title_zh: China threatened the US with a response to the new tariffs – what is at stake for the trade truce between Beijing and Washington
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a new wave of tariffs on the European Union, China and other trade partners, the result of a probe into what it says are unfair manufacturing practices.
Some of the proposals include tariffs of at least 20% on China, which would match an agreement reached with the White House. But the duties could reach up to 40% if talks between the two countries fail.
The United States’ current trade truce with China was recently extended and is set to expire in January.
The tariffs will be implemented under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a statute that the White House has relied upon more frequently for trade authority ever since the Supreme Court blocked many of Trump’s 2025 country-specific tariffs, imposed under a different authority.
Wednesday’s announcement came less than a month after Trump’s tariff policies — and the inflation they fueled — contributed to Republicans’ sweeping losses in the midterm elections. Inflation hit 3.7% in September, driven primarily by energy prices, but also by higher prices of goods.
In announcing the details of the new duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the overall rates applied to each trading partner would not surpass levels that were previously agreed to as part of bilateral framework trade deals.
“When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points,” Greer said on CNBC.
“So what we’re proposing today are actually a set of targeted tariffs to respond to this problem of excess capacity,” he added.
For example, Trump agreed to cap tariffs on E.U. imports at 15% as part of a deal reached in 2025. On Wednesday, the trade representative reiterated that cap.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for the case of China.
“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this,” Greer said. “They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple of months from now.”
He said he expects that “a broad” negotiation with trading partners would follow Wednesday’s proposals.
But tensions continue to flare with trading partners, especially between Canada, the E.U. and China.
Overnight, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry rejected the basis for the new tariffs. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said in a briefing for reporters.
“So-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false proposition,” the spokesperson added. “China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation.”
Separately, the European Union said its members “strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity.”
The bloc shares the Trump administration’s concerns about overcapacity, said Olof Gill, deputy chief spokesman for the the European Commission. Given the mutual concerns, the E.U.  regrets “the lack of joint action” with the United States to address the problem.
Just weeks ago, Greer accused the E.U. of “aggressively” supporting Airbus and said that a loan from the European Investment Bank to the French aerospace giant threatened to inject “substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector.”
The E.U. rejected Greer’s assertion, saying the loan was normal and he had “really no grounds” to question it. The bloc, made up of 27 countries, is America’s largest trading partner.
Meanwhile, in August, trade talks with Canada collapsed after Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump administration requested “uneconomic” and unfair terms at the last minute.
Carney recalled his negotiators to Ottawa and for more than three months the two sides have traded verbal barbs. Canada is the country’s third-largest trading partner, according to data through September.
Recently, informal talks resumed between the U.S. and Canada but a formal deal does not yet appear to be within reach.
On Wednesday, Greer said those talks with Canada were continuing, due to some outstanding “sticking points.”
Another key U.S. trading partner, Mexico, was not included in Wednesday’s tariff proposals.
“I think the most important one where we’re still going through the investigation process, is Mexico,” Greer told CNBC. “I think it’ll be a little bit more time before we release that report,” he said.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: FCC approves 1 million SpaceX data centers in space. Astronomers are dismayed.
articles.title_zh: FCC approves 1 million SpaceX data centers in space. Astronomers are dismayed.
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites in space for the creation of data centers critical to powering artificial intelligence.
The decision comes as the US races to lead the world in AI, a technology that promises to turbocharge innovation and economic growth. Harnessing AI is also central to SpaceX’s growth ambitions, though the company cautioned in a regulatory filing ahead of its June initial public offering that launching data centers in space relied on “unproven” technologies and “may not achieve commercial viability.”
Deploying SpaceX’s “Starmind” constellation – comprised of 1 million orbital compute modules – will help meet “rapidly growing demand” for AI computing power, the FCC said in a statement Wednesday. The deployed satellites will “process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the agency added.
“This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
AI data centers require enormous amounts of energy and Musk has endorsed orbital data centers that can harness the power of the sun.
“By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost ​and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX ​told the FCC when it applied for permission to launch the satellites earlier this year.
Musk welcomed the decision, saying on X, his social media platform, that “this will be a great asset to America and the world.”
The initiative has drawn criticism from the scientific community, however, who have argued that the technology could disrupt views of the night sky and increase pollution. In a statement Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society said it was “dismayed” by the FCC’s decision, which it had opposed in earlier filings to the agency.
The “proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the organization said.
It noted that the satellites would be visible as “extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky” and would generate “radio emissions” and “waste heat” that would “threaten… sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research.” It also warned of “atmospheric pollution” from the launches and reentries so many satellites.
Under the license, SpaceX must deploy at least one authorized space station by November 2033, deploy 10% of the total – or 100,000 – by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038.
There are currently around 16,700 operational satellites in space, according to Orbital Radar , a platform providing real-time tracking of objects in orbit. The European Space Agency puts the number of functioning satellites slightly lower, at 15,800.
Earlier this month, in a historic test flight , SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft deployed Starlink internet satellites before returning to earth and pulling of an unprecedented landing.

articles.title_orig: Final New Zealand election vote count to confirm parliament make up
articles.title_zh: Final New Zealand election vote count to confirm parliament make up
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden , moving to Australia.

articles.title_orig: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child in $18 billion AI charm offensive
articles.title_zh: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child in $18 billion AI charm offensive
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account , and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active.
Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added.
Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov.
Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift.
SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December .
In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year.
Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.
Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.
Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts . Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported.
Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.
The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations , a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts.
Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.
Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17.
SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla . The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal.
CNBC's Sam Meredith, Kevin Breuninger, Kate Dore and Jess Dickler contributed to this story

articles.title_zh: Nate Silver predicts Trump ‘absolutely’ could be impeached over Nvidia’s China chip sales
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Polling analyst Nate Silver has predicted that President Donald Trump “absolutely” could be impeached over the sale of Nvidia’s AI chips to China .
As the scandal of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese spy unfolded last week, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released more eyebrow-raising information. The Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to alleged Chinese military-backed companies.
After Democrats crushed Republicans in the midterms earlier this month, they have vowed to hold the Trump administration accountable. But will they try to kick Trump out of office over his ties to Nvidia? Silver said there’s definitely a chance.
“Do you know what the prediction markets say for what's the chance that Trump will be impeached and removed from office before his term ends?” Silver asked his co-hosts on the Still Counting podcast.
“Are they saying it’s like 25 percent? I have not looked,” Galen Druke guessed.
Silver said Druke was “uncannily accurate,” adding that he thinks it’s “entirely reasonable” that there’s a 25 percent chance the House adopts articles of impeachment against Trump and the Senate votes to convict him.
But their co-host, Clare Malone, disagreed that Trump — who was impeached by the House and acquitted by the Senate twice during his first term — would be removed from office in his second term, saying the betting markets are “addled.”
“If he is aiding and abetting, he could absolutely get removed by the Senate,” Silver continued. “If his approval keeps going down at the rate it is, he’s going to be at whatever 29 percent by the end of next year. And if he’s doing s*** to like profit off selling advanced chips to China, abso-f***ing-lutely he could be removed — and he should be.”
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife on November 8 after The New York Times reported that he had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center whom U.S. intelligence suspected of feeding information to Beijing.
When the Nvidia scandal broke, Trump said he was “amazed” by the news “because I view [Huang] as a very high quality person. I've known him a long time.”
Huang stepped down as CEO on Nov. 12 , causing Nvidia’s stock to plummet. After shareholders and Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley , including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, called for the Nvidia founder to be brought back at the helm, the company’s board announced Monday that it unanimously agreed to reinstate him .
It was reported that Trump had a hand in Huang’s return, with three people familiar with the matter telling CNBC that Huang had not broken national security laws.
“I convinced them,” Trump admitted to CNBC. “We believe he’s fine. He’s absolutely fine.”
Trump made up to $15 million on Nvidia shares Monday as the company’s stock price spiked over the news of Huang’s return, the Financial Times reported.
Trump, who raked in about $2.2 billion last year, has denied profiting off the presidency, telling 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat earlier this month, “I devote almost no time to my net worth.”

articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and President Trump speak to reporters aboard Air Force One. Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.
Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.
Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of  a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.
Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.
The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.
What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.
Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title_orig: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
articles.title_zh: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people .
The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.
The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.
In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.
The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.
Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.
The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.
The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.
By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.
“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”
A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.
“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”
The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.
The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.
President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.
“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.
Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.
The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.
Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.
Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.
“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.
Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.
Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.

articles.title_orig: Heavy Rain, Wind And Flooding Hit Much Of The U.S. On Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Heavy Rain, Wind And Flooding Hit Much Of The U.S. On Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
Fearless reporting isn’t optional — it’s essential. Back our year-end push to power 2027 coverage (and read ad-free as a Gold or Platinum member).
Already a member? Log in to hide these messages.
Holiday storms flooded East Coast communities, knocked out power to nearly a million customers and prompted the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade .
High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, snarling holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity Thursday evening, with the majority in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us. Over 2,200 flights to or from U.S. destinations were delayed and more than 400 were canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.
Macy’s postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade’s massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers.
Torrential rain, high winds and flooding pounded sections of the East Coast. New Jersey was under a state of emergency, along with parts of New York. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.
Two people were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday morning, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said.
The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, Borough of Avalon Business Administrator Scott J. Wahl said.
“Not quite Hurricane Sandy,” Wahl said of the benchmark storm for his village on the far south end of New Jersey’s Atlantic coast.
Floodwaters washed debris over the road, and a few drivers were rescued after driving around barricades into floodwaters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.
Lance Miller, 54, said floodwaters in his Ocean City, New Jersey, neighborhood were about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest supermarket would probably “destroy your car.”
Miller said he would be staying indoors and having Thanksgiving dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends were “not so lucky” and had flooding inside their homes.
The Margate City Fire Department near Atlantic City, New Jersey, posted video on Facebook of water pouring through the city’s streets, even before heavy rains started.
A firefighter said the tide was coming in ferociously, even with an hour to go before its peak. Water closed in on houses, and sandbags were piled in front of businesses.
Some highways and bridges were temporarily closed. The nearly 18-mile (29-kilometer) Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in southern Virginia was closed for several hours Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes and covered the two-lane highway.
In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm.
The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings on Thursday, including a rare twister southeast of Seattle, Washington.
President Donald Trump signed a disaster declaration Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues. Trump had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach.
Trump was asked about aid for Thursday’s storms on the East Coast. “Well, we’re going to look at that. We have some requests from others,” he said.
Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St. Louis recording 7.3 inches (18.5 centimeters) of snowfall. Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, recorded 14 inches.
The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 a.m., according to the city.
Meanwhile, high-tide driven waves and strong winds caused flooding along the Pacific coast Thursday. The conditions were expected into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.
King tides were surging along the West Coast.
Video showed a massive wave tearing down part of the Pacifica pier in California on Wednesday, sending it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped pier in the summer after finding cracks.
Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner posted more than a dozen itinerary changes on social media Thursday morning, starting with one that said trains could not run through San Clemente “due to track damage.” It also suspended service between Irvine and Oceanside because of washouts caused by high tide conditions. Service was further shut down from San Diego north to Oceanside and up to Los Angeles International Airport.
Josh Boak in West Palm Beach, Florida contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Hamas in talks with Palestinian factions over Israeli targeted killings in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Hamas in talks with Palestinian factions over Israeli targeted killings in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya said that the terrorist organization was holding consultations with other Palestinian factions on how to respond to a recent series of Israeli targeted killings of senior Hamas officials in the Gaza Strip.
“The equation of continued killing and siege under an agreement is unacceptable to us. We are holding discussions with the other Palestinian factions on how to respond to the daily killings directed against us,” al-Hayya said.
Al-Hayya did not specify what measures Hamas and the other Palestinian factions were considering in response to the Israeli strikes.
His remarks came after the IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) confirmed on Thursday that they had killed senior Hamas political bureau official Khaled Abu Nada in a strike in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip.
Abu Nada headed Hamas's Economic Department and served as the terrorist organization's education minister. According to the military, he was responsible for managing Hamas's banking and investment systems and directing funds toward terrorist activities and the rehabilitation of its military capabilities.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz said in a joint statement on Thursday that Israel would continue targeting members of Hamas's leadership.
“No terrorist is immune, and no one in the Hamas leadership will manage to evade us,” Netanyahu and Katz said.
On Wednesday, the IDF and Shin Bet confirmed the killing of Muhammad Majed Abu al-Ouf , the head of Hamas's internal security apparatus in the northern Gaza Strip.
According to the military, Abu al-Ouf was involved in efforts to restore Hamas's operational capabilities and had overseen executions of Palestinians who opposed the terrorist organization's rule.
The strike followed the killing of Naeem Abu Nahel , the head of Hamas's internal security apparatus in the Gaza Strip, which Netanyahu and Katz confirmed on Tuesday.
Hamas condemned Abu Nahel's killing and called on the international community to pressure Israel to adhere to the ceasefire agreement.
The targeted killings come amid ongoing international efforts to advance the implementation of US President Donald Trump's peace plan for the Gaza Strip, including the disarmament of Hamas and the establishment of an alternative governing authority.
On Monday, the Board of Peace announced that Hamas and other Palestinian factions had agreed to a disarmament roadmap, providing for the relinquishment of their weapons and the transfer of civilian and security responsibilities to a transitional Palestinian administration.
However, the board acknowledged that implementation remained limited, calling on both Israel and Hamas to fulfill their commitments under the agreement.

articles.title_orig: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
articles.title_zh: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account , and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active.
Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added.
Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov.
Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift.
SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December .
In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year.
Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.
Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.
Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts . Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported.
Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.
The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations , a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts.
Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.
Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17.
SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla . The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal.
CNBC's Sam Meredith, Kevin Breuninger, Kate Dore and Jess Dickler contributed to this story

articles.title_orig: Microsoft: Salt Typhoon’s ARTEX wins access ‘in a matter of minutes’
articles.title_zh: Microsoft: Salt Typhoon’s ARTEX wins access ‘in a matter of minutes’
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York
State-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft says. Microsoft Threat Intelligence named the groups in a report published on Wednesday .
The list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean. Two more clusters, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358, are also on it. Microsoft says state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers use ARTEX to speed up network scans, credential attacks, and attacks on web apps.
“Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes,” Microsoft wrote.
The report landed hours after US media tied ARTEX to the hack of three US spy agencies , as Jonathan Greig reported for The Record .
US agencies believe Salt Typhoon breached at least nine telecoms groups in 2024, The Record noted. That hack allegedly reached phones used by Donald Trump and JD Vance. A US House report later said Chinese carriers were still inside American phone networks .
Crystal Typhoon is newer. It was first seen in late 2023 and goes after government networks and critical infrastructure through edge devices and firewalls, TechRadar reported .
Microsoft had already linked Storm-0940 to the ConnectWise supply chain attack . The new report adds numbers from its campaigns. In one, Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 a minute. In several intrusions, the attackers had privileged access less than three hours after they first went after a target.
In another case, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.
A GitHub user called Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese interface in July. The developer took it down in October, but other developers kept publishing their own versions. This month, the Chinese security firm ThreatBook claimed ownership and started selling access to “ARTEX Pro”.
The attacker sets the targets. One AI model breaks the job into goals. A planner agent then hands short tasks to worker agents with a real shell and hacking tools. A reporter agent writes up what worked. ARTEX can run on almost any large language model, including ones stripped of their guardrails. That means no single AI provider’s safety controls can stop it, Microsoft says.
The FBI warned about ARTEX earlier this month.
“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.
Attackers can change the tool’s IP addresses and user agent strings, so blocking those alone will not work. The steadiest sign is behaviour: many varied requests in a short burst, and quick moves to the next step. ARTEX does nothing to hide that activity by default.
Microsoft also suggests honeypots, tarpits, and fake wins. A fake win shows the agent false proof that its job is done, so it stops. It recommends rate limits, phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in, and replacing any secret that leaks into code. The report also points customers to Microsoft’s own products, including Defender XDR and its Perception security agents.
